source.title: Regularization in ResNet with Stochastic Depth

record.file_problem: Text contains the full paper and appendix. Some equations and table formatting are flattened, but the main CIFAR tables are recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests explicit and implicit regularization effects of stochastic depth, including reported CIFAR test-error comparisons across survival-rate modes. It does not test the listed versions directly, but its natural-label generalization results bear on the claim’s subject.
record.gate_note: Rows cover CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 test errors for stochastic-depth survival-rate modes under fixed training budgets. The paper’s theoretical analyses of regularization, gradient growth, Gaussianity, and approximation accuracy are not rows for the listed versions because they do not directly measure their named behaviors. Values used to choose survival rates are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes stochastic depth and compares survival-probability schedules. None of its own results tests V1–V8. Dropping residual blocks is distinct from the neuron dropout named in V6; its flatness argument does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its correlation with generalization gaps as required by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: stochastic depth induces explicit loss regularization and, under stated assumptions and approximations, asymptotically Gaussian activation and gradient noise. They interpret their CIFAR experiments as supporting SenseMode for small average-depth budgets and uniform schedules for large budgets, with a budget–performance trade-off. This is a general tendency rather than a universal ordering: Table 6 includes exceptions for ResNet56.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use stochastic-depth ResNets with a 1/√L stable scaling and compare survival-rate modes; the listed versions concern other interventions or measurements. The main image-classification experiments use SGD with momentum and report test error, not training error.
record.method_sensitivity: Survival-rate mode and budget ratio change the reported test error; the preferred mode differs between low and high budget regimes and by dataset/model.

fits_no_version.finding: For Stable ResNet110, SenseMode has lower mean test error than uniform survival probabilities at budget ratios 0.1–0.4 on both CIFAR datasets. Uniform has lower mean error at 0.5–0.9, tying linear at 0.9 on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative test performance of stochastic-depth survival schedules depends on average subnetwork depth; SenseMode can improve low-budget performance, while uniform schedules generally perform better at larger budgets.

record.code_released: https://github.com/felixgwu/img_classification_pk_pytorch (base implementation); supplementary code/notebooks mentioned, URL not stated
record.problems: The experiment reports test error without corresponding training error, so it does not measure the train–test gap. The main table reports four-run averages with standard deviations; the text does not provide statistical tests. The table values do not establish the claim versions’ random-label, width-scaling, architecture-comparison, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example effects.
record.rows_left_out: None. Kept the separately reported mode-by-budget test-error outcomes for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 in Table 2, within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out performance compared with natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error across widths beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations. Average subnetwork depth is not batch size.
Neuron dropout versus no dropout, training-set-size dependence, excessive-dropout underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, measured train–test gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The rows' exclusion follows from their intervention and comparison, not merely the absence of training-error measurements. They may be retained as findings outside the listed versions, but should not serve as claim-evidence rows. The record's rows_left_out statement overlooks Table 2's no-SD baselines and Table 6's ResNet56 results; neither supplies a test of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test accuracy under the same training recipes.
Width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold and test error as width increases.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the effect of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to the training recipe.
Dropout versus no dropout and the stated training-set-size and underfitting conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train–test gaps versus other measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
